h1: Table turns at a brewpub and how they shape revenue
title: Table Turns and Brewpub Revenue | Craft Beer School
desc: What table turns are, how to measure them at a brewpub and how turn time, group size and spend interact to shape revenue on busy and quiet nights.
teaser: Two brewpubs with the same seats and the same menu can earn very different amounts. The difference is often how often each table is used.
standfirst: Table turns measure how many times a seat is used in a session. In a brewpub, where guests linger over beer, turns behave differently from a quick-service restaurant. This guide shows how to measure them and when to push them.
sections:
A table turn is one complete use of a table: guests sit, order, eat or drink, pay and leave. Then the table is reset for the next group. If a table is used three times in an evening, it turned three times. The average turn rate is total covers divided by total seats over a session.

So a 100-seat brewpub that serves 180 covers on a Friday evening has a turn rate of 1.8. The same room serving 60 covers on a Tuesday has a turn rate of 0.6. Both numbers matter, but they need different fixes.
Why brewpubs turn slower than restaurants

A brewpub is a place people come to stay. A group may order a tasting flight, then a pint each, then food, then another round. That is good for spend per head. It is slow for turns. A quick-service café might turn a table several times an hour. A brewpub table at peak might turn once every two hours.

That is not a flaw. A guest who stays longer and spends more can be worth more than two guests who leave quickly. The useful measure is revenue per seat per hour, which captures both spend and speed.

Divide revenue for a session by the number of seats multiplied by the hours open. Suppose a 100-seat room takes a given sum over a five hour evening. Revenue per seat hour is that sum divided by 500. Track the figure for each day and each part of the day.

This number tells you where the room earns and where it idles. It often shows that a busy Saturday from 8 to 11 pm earns far more per seat hour than the whole of a weekday afternoon. That is the basis for decisions on opening hours, happy hours and staffing.
When to push turns and when to leave them

Pushing turns only makes sense when there is a queue. On a Friday night with a waiting list, a table that lingers for three hours over one round costs the venue a second group. On a Tuesday, pushing anyone out is pointless and rude.

Ways to speed turns politely at peak:

  • Take orders quickly and bring the first beer within a few minutes.
  • Fire food promptly and clear plates as soon as guests finish.
  • Present the bill when asked, without delay. Make payment fast with card or UPI at the table.
  • Use time-limited bookings at peak, stated at booking.

Never rush guests at the expense of hospitality. A regular who feels hurried does not come back.

Turns are also lost to seat mismatch. A couple at a six-top wastes four seats for two hours. Track the size of your groups by day of week. If most Friday groups are four to six people and your tables seat two, you will turn people away while seats sit empty.

Bookings help here. Our guide on table booking and delivery apps covers what they cost, which you can weigh against the extra covers they bring.
Average spend and turns pull against each other

Every move that speeds a table can also shrink the bill. Bring the bill too early and the group skips the second round. Remove the dessert menu to save time and the average spend falls. The aim is not the highest turn rate. It is the highest revenue per seat hour across the whole session.

Beer helps here. A server who recommends a second pint or a flight of the seasonal beers raises spend without slowing the table much, because pouring takes a minute and the guest was staying anyway. Our guide on training bar staff to sell craft beer covers how to do that without pushing anyone to drink more than they want.

More turns means more covers per server, more orders to the kitchen and more glasses through the washer. A floor team that copes with 1.0 turns may fall apart at 2.0. Map your staffing against expected covers by hour, not just by shift.

The kitchen sets a hard limit. If the line can send out 60 plates an hour, that caps how fast tables can turn on food. Pouring is quicker, which is one reason beer-led brewpubs can turn faster than food-led ones.

Most POS systems record when a table opens and closes. Export a week of data and calculate covers, average turn time and revenue per seat hour for each day. You will see within an hour where the room is earning and where it is not. That is better than any industry average.

The Brewery Business Management course covers revenue modelling, staffing and pricing for brewpubs, with turns as one input. Pick your busiest night and measure average turn time from seat to bill before you change anything.
faqs: What is a good table turn rate for a brewpub?
There is no single figure. Brewpubs turn slower than restaurants because guests linger. Track your own revenue per seat hour and compare days and sessions.
How do I calculate table turns?
Divide covers served in a session by the number of seats. A 100-seat room serving 180 covers has a turn rate of 1.8.
Should a brewpub try to increase table turns?
Only at peak, when there is a queue. On quiet nights a guest who stays and spends more is worth keeping.
